reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
clinicalPearls: True hepatic infarction is uncommon because of the liver's dual blood supply from the hepatic artery and portal vein.
Compromise of the hepatic artery is the usual precipitant, and hepatic artery thrombosis is a dreaded early complication after liver transplantation.

Other causes include arterial embolism, vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa, hypercoagulable states, aortic dissection, trauma and iatrogenic injury during hepatobiliary surgery or transarterial therapy.
Obstetric catastrophes such as HELLP syndrome and eclampsia can produce hepatic infarction alongside hepatic haematoma.
Typical features are sudden right upper quadrant pain, fever and a brisk rise in transaminases.
Contrast CT shows characteristic wedge-shaped or geographic peripheral hypodense areas that fail to enhance, while Doppler ultrasound and angiography assess arterial patency.
Post-transplant arterial thrombosis is a surgical emergency requiring urgent revascularisation or consideration of re-transplantation.
Infarcted tissue may liquefy and become secondarily infected, forming an abscess or biloma.
reference.pathophysiology: The liver's dual perfusion normally protects it from ischaemic necrosis, so infarction usually requires either occlusion of the hepatic artery when portal inflow is already compromised, or a profound reduction in total hepatic blood flow. When arterial supply is lost the biliary tree, which depends almost entirely on the hepatic artery, is especially vulnerable, so ischaemic cholangiopathy and bile leaks may accompany parenchymal necrosis. Thrombosis, embolism, external compression, vasculitic occlusion or surgical interruption produce a segmental, wedge-shaped zone of coagulative necrosis whose apex points towards the hilum and base towards the capsule. The necrotic focus incites an inflammatory response and may subsequently undergo liquefaction, secondary infection or, if the patient survives, fibrosis and atrophy of the affected segment.
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic artery and portal vein
Liver function tests with serial transaminases
Blood cultures if secondary infection is suspected
Echocardiography to seek an embolic source
redFlags: Post-transplant setting with rising transaminases, indicating arterial thrombosis until proven otherwise
Signs of sepsis suggesting an infected infarct or biloma
Rapidly progressive hepatic dysfunction or fulminant failure
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the cause and extent, with small infarcts in a native liver often healing on supportive care, whereas post-transplant arterial thrombosis carries high morbidity and frequently requires re-transplantation.
pitfalls: Attributing a post-transplant transaminase rise to rejection and missing arterial thrombosis.
Delaying Doppler assessment of arterial patency when infarction is suspected.
Mistaking a wedge-shaped infarct for an abscess or tumour on imaging.
Overlooking an underlying vasculitis or thrombophilia in a native liver.
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Treat the underlying cause: urgent revascularisation for hepatic artery thrombosis, anticoagulation for thrombotic or hypercoagulable states, immunosuppression for vasculitis, and expedited delivery for HELLP syndrome or eclampsia
After liver transplantation, manage hepatic artery thrombosis with urgent surgical or endovascular revascularisation, and consider re-transplantation if the graft is not salvageable
Provide supportive care with analgesia, fluid resuscitation, and correction of coagulopathy
Give antibiotics and drain any secondary infection or abscess complicating the necrotic segment
Monitor serial transaminases and reassess arterial and portal patency with Doppler ultrasound or angiography
Screen for ischaemic cholangiopathy and bile leak, which follow loss of arterial supply to the biliary tree
Manage jointly with hepatology and transplant or hepatobiliary surgery and investigate for a thrombophilia
